At the declared notes entry, the action uses the supplied request user and binds the requested document, first checks view_document, then checks change_document for POST, and only afterward creates the Note and performs the subsequent update/search work. The supplied caller has the global permissions and object change grant, so the strongest visible authorization control for this scenario passes whether the owner is absent or is another user. Source behavior is therefore observed allow. This matches the accepted policy's allow branch because the non-owner caller has an object change_document grant; the object view grant alone is not being used as the decisive basis. Any database/store failure or later effect failure would be an external execution outcome, not an authorization result. Source discovery is not-tested, so this is not a repository-wide completeness claim.

def has_perms_owner_aware(user, perms, obj):
    """
    Legacy slow path (guardian-backed) single-object permission check.

    The queryset-filtering side of this migrated onto
    ``PermittedObjectsFilter``/``permitted_object_ids()``, but this
    single-object check still has many production callers. Several callers
    remain across ``documents/``, ``paperless_mail/``, and ``paperless_ai/``
    -- grep for this function name before removing it.
    """
    checker = ObjectPermissionChecker(user)
    return obj.owner is None or obj.owner == user or checker.has_perm(perms, obj)

citations.quote:
# Guardian's UserObjectPermission/GroupObjectPermission always store a bare
    # codename, but has_perm()-style callers commonly pass the qualified
    # "app_label.codename" form. content_type already disambiguates the
    # codename, so just drop any prefix rather than silently under-permitting.
    perm = perm.rsplit(".", 1)[-1]

    content_type = ContentType.objects.get_for_model(model)
    perm_filter = {
        "permission__codename": perm,
        "permission__content_type": content_type,
    }

    user_perm_ids = (
        UserObjectPermission.objects.filter(user=user, **perm_filter)
        .annotate(object_pk_int=Cast("object_pk", IntegerField()))
        .values_list("object_pk_int", flat=True)
    )
    group_perm_ids = (
        GroupObjectPermission.objects.filter(group__user=user, **perm_filter)
        .annotate(object_pk_int=Cast("object_pk", IntegerField()))
        .values_list("object_pk_int", flat=True)
    )
    permitted_ids = user_perm_ids.union(group_perm_ids)

    return base_qs.filter(
        Q(owner=user) | Q(owner__isnull=True) | Q(id__in=permitted_ids),
    ).values_list("id", flat=True)

The declared entry binds the request user and document, performs the view_document gate, and for POST performs the owner-aware change_document gate before the Note creation effect. With an absent owner, the source predicate itself permits the object; with another owner and no object change grant, it blocks the effect. Because owner presence is unspecified in the current scenario and changes the source-visible result, the current observed behavior is unknown. The minimum decisive source-external fact is whether the bound document's owner is null or is a different user. Under the accepted policy, the non-owner caller with only an object view grant should be denied in either branch because ownership and an object change_document grant are both absent; the absent-owner source allowance is a source/policy discrepancy, not evidence that the accepted policy allows it. Any database/store failure would be an execution outcome, not authorization. Source discovery is not-tested, so no repository-wide completeness claim is made.
